notes:
Need to search first.I could only use part of what I planned. The tool limit ran out after two searches, so I never opened the full pages. These notes rest on the parts of 7 pages that the search tool returned, and mostly on 3 of them: Enduring Word (David Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, and two of Bible Hub's verse pages (Acts 11:1 and 11:21). On Bible Hub's combined pages, some excerpts didn't show which commentator wrote them. I've marked those "author not shown" rather than guess.

Here is what's missing, so you can fill it in later:
- **Verses with nothing found:** vv. 5–11, 13–14 and 27–30. The Enduring Word section on vv. 27–30 was cut off, and I found nothing at all on Agabus or Claudius.
- **Reading by reading:** I didn't reach Ellicott's notes on most verses, Gill's beyond vv. 1 and 19–21, Precept Austin, or the NET Bible notes.
- **Section 2 (Protestant differences):** I couldn't search for any tradition's own teachers. That means nothing from Pentecostal, Methodist, Lutheran or Baptist sources on Spirit baptism (vv. 15–17), on how repentance is "granted" (v. 18), or on household salvation (v. 14).
- **Section 3 (other views):** No Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or popular-teaching sources. The only related material is a Protestant commentary's remarks about the papacy, under vv. 3–4 below.

---

**v. 1**
- News of Gentiles believing at Caesarea couldn't be kept quiet, and nobody tried to hide it, even though it would confuse and offend many Jewish believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- The news would have spread fast to the centre of Jewish Christianity and caused a stir. Luke doesn't say what James and the other apostles thought. The Greek is better rendered "throughout Judea" (Vincent's Word Studies, quoted on the same page). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/11-1.htm
- One commentary on that page (author not shown) says the news alarmed them. These weren't Jews living abroad or converts to Judaism. They were uncircumcised Gentiles, baptized and welcomed without being required to keep the Law of Moses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/11-1.htm

**v. 2**
- "The circumcision" is an odd label at a time when every church member was Jewish. The Pulpit Commentary thinks it reflects Luke's own Gentile background and his aim of recording how Gentile Christianity grew. Peter had come back to Jerusalem, wanting to talk the matter over with the other apostles, and was attacked straight away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- One commentary on the Bible Hub page (author not shown) thinks there's no reason to exclude any Jewish believers from the dispute, except perhaps the apostles, since all of them were zealous for the Law. It notes that Peter had felt the same way before his vision, and that he later pulled back from Gentile believers (Galatians 2:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/11-1.htm
- Peter's decision to take six witnesses to Caesarea proved wise, given this reaction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 3**
- The complaint was about what Peter did (eating with Gentiles), not at first about what God was doing among them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- Acts 10 doesn't actually record the meal, but it almost certainly happened. The Pulpit Commentary says the accusers treated it as the worst part of the report. It adds that Peter shows no sign of "papal domination," a Protestant remark on Peter's authority. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm

**v. 4**
- Peter's account is a shortened version of Acts 10:9–43, and the repetition shows how important the events were. Guzik quotes James Boice: Peter didn't flaunt his authority as an apostle but humbly told the facts, carefully and in order. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- One Pulpit Commentary homily says Peter wasn't silenced by force. He was held to account as one member of the church, and what settled the matter was the Spirit's work shown in facts and reliable witnesses. Another sermon there says Peter told facts that could have been checked, and named his six companions as witnesses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/acts/11.htm
- A Pulpit Commentary sermon on StudyLight, written from a Protestant view of church authority, says the church here accepts the rule of the Spirit, not any "earthly lord" or "vicar of Christ." It also notes that the church gave Peter a patient hearing and accepted his account of the facts. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/acts-11.html

**vv. 5–10**
- Guzik: Peter first thought the vision was about food, but came to see it was about people (Acts 10:28). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- The Pulpit Commentary sermon on StudyLight names the main barrier: a Jew's deep-rooted dislike, reinforced by upbringing, of things considered common or unclean. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/acts-11.html

**v. 12**
- Newer editions of the Greek text read "making no distinction" where older ones read "nothing doubting." The same verb appears in Acts 15:9, where God "made no distinction" between Jews and Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- Guzik: Peter stresses that an angel had stood in Cornelius's house first. If an angel could go in, so could Peter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 15**
- The Spirit falling "as upon us at the beginning" was God's stamp of approval. The Jewish believers couldn't withhold acceptance once God had given his. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 16**
- Peter is recalling Acts 1:5. The Pulpit Commentary suggests this may mean Peter supplied Luke with many details for chapters 1–12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- Guzik: the believers could see this agreed with Scripture, both Jesus' word (Mark 1:8) and Old Testament promises that Gentiles would come to the Messiah (e.g. Isaiah 49:6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 17**
- "Who was I that I could withstand God?" uses the same Greek verb as "Can anyone forbid water?" in Acts 10:47. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- Guzik's lesson: notice where God is working and go that way, rather than trying to pull God toward our own preferences. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 18**
- First came stunned silence, then praise. Guzik: the Jerusalem believers' hearts were soft enough for God's word and work to overcome their prejudice and tradition. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- The Pulpit Commentary says God's way of doing this calmed Jewish prejudice and kept the church at peace. Even so, the exclusive spirit lasted a long time, as Acts 15, Galatians 2 and Philippians 3 show. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm

**v. 19**
- Ellicott calls this the start of a new and important section. One commentary on the page (author not shown) says they preached only to Jews because they weren't yet convinced Gentiles were called, with God letting them see it step by step. Gill gives geographical notes on Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/11-19.htm
- The story goes back to the persecution of Acts 8:1. Antioch had a large Jewish population, and Josephus counted it the third city of the empire after Rome and Alexandria. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm

**v. 20**
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers the reading "Greeks" over "Grecians" (Greek-speaking Jews). Its reason is that these people are contrasted with those who preached only to Jews, and reaching Greek-speaking Jews would have been nothing new. They were probably uncircumcised Gentiles who feared God, like Cornelius. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- Guzik calls the unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene genuine heroes: they began the first deliberate mission to Gentiles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 21**
- "The hand of the Lord" means God's power working with them and through them, like the Old Testament phrase "a mighty hand." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- Gill, a Calvinist Baptist, says the many conversions came not from the preachers' persuasion or the hearers' free will, but from God's power and "efficacious grace." In his view God acts in conversion and man is passive; "turned to the Lord" then means obedience that follows faith. This is a clearly Reformed reading. I found no Wesleyan or other answer to it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/11-21.htm
- Another commentary on that page (author not shown) says faith is claimed in vain where heart and life don't change. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/11-21.htm
- Guzik: you can't turn people to the Lord without the Lord's hand. "Believed and turned" describes both faith and repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 22**
- The Pulpit Commentary says sending Barnabas, a friend of Saul who favoured preaching to Gentiles, suggests Jerusalem had already accepted Peter's report. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm

**v. 23**
- "The grace of God" means the number and genuineness of the conversions. Barnabas lives up to his name, "son of encouragement." "Cleave unto" means abide or persevere, and the Pulpit Commentary says such warnings show the real danger of falling away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- Guzik: Barnabas focused on building up the church, in line with Ephesians 4:11–16. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- A Pulpit Commentary sermon on StudyLight says what mattered was God's grace, not the human channel it came through. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/acts-11.html

**v. 24**
- "Good" means moral goodness. Barnabas is described in the same terms as Stephen (Acts 6:5), and the Spirit here is the power behind his preaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm

**v. 25**
- Earlier hostility had driven Saul to Tarsus, which the Pulpit Commentary sees as God's providence, since it put him close to Antioch. It also quotes Lewin's dating of about ten years after the crucifixion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/11.htm
- "To seek" means to hunt him up. Guzik quotes MacArthur that it suggests a hard search. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/

**v. 26**
- Antioch combined formal teaching (Barnabas and Saul) with ordinary believers witnessing informally, and Guzik credits that mix with the church's impact. He thinks "Christian" probably began as a mocking name, which believers took up because their main identity now belonged to Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- A Pulpit Commentary sermon on StudyLight links the new name to the church's mission to the wider world. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/acts-11.html

**vv. 29–30**
- Guzik: each person giving as they were able shows that true discipleship overflows in generosity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-11/
- A Pulpit Commentary sermon on StudyLight calls self-sacrifice the test of real unity. Wealthy Antioch helped poor Judea, which proved the Gentile converts were truly part of the apostles' church. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/acts-11.html
